lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on how the news lost its way
lead.head: Eight crises, no villains

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma early in Episode 113

body: Ajay Shah grew up among jour­nal­ists. From the age of six, he lived in a hous­ing com­plex where 80 house­holds all worked in the Indian media, and to him the trade was “fully a noble call­ing”. {113-S01}

Amit Varma, who came to jour­nal­ism by ac­ci­dent around 2001, saw a more com­pli­cated world. Here he set out what went wrong, as eight crises: of rel­e­vance, pur­pose, money, qual­ity, trust, power, in­cen­tives and at­ten­tion.

He in­sisted the story had no vil­lains, only struc­tures and in­cen­tives. He had pre­pared by talk­ing again to three jour­nal­ists who had been guests on his pod­cast, *The Seen and the Unseen*: Prem Panicker, Shephali Bhatt and Samarth Bansal.
## Too much in­for­ma­tion
Journalism began, Varma ar­gued, be­cause in­for­ma­tion was scarce. A town crier of­fered a tiny nugget in the evening, and peo­ple val­ued who­ever brought it. That is no longer true. {113-C01}

“Today in­for­ma­tion is abun­dant,” he said. “There is prac­ti­cally too much in­for­ma­tion.” The old in­sti­tu­tions linger like arte­facts, and peo­ple swip­ing on Instagram are not to blame: their needs are met else­where.

Shah ob­jected that truth is still scarce, be­cause cor­po­ra­tions, gov­ern­ments and par­ties or­gan­ise them­selves to lie. Varma agreed that a good news­pa­per should fil­ter for the truth, but said the main­stream media had ab­di­cated that role.
## Follow the money

Purpose col­lided with profit. A news­pa­per is a busi­ness with share­hold­ers, Varma said, and news­rooms came to be treated as cost cen­tres. One ed­i­tor told a jour­nal­ist he spoke to that the job was to com­fort the com­forted.

Then the in­ter­net made ad­ver­tis­ing the only way to earn on­line, with the page view as its unit. As sites mul­ti­plied, page views lost value, the way money does when its sup­ply grows. {113-C04}

A race to the bot­tom fol­lowed: click­bait, SEO head­lines, ar­ti­cles chopped into pages. Senior peo­ple were sacked, spe­cial­ist beats were cut, and re­porters be­came gen­er­al­ists fil­ing three sto­ries a day.

Shah of­fered the clean­est ev­i­dence. Bennett Coleman, long the one Indian media house that re­li­ably made money, went all in on tabloids and click­bait. Its op­er­at­ing profit fell sig­nif­i­cantly.

Quality was never as high as nos­tal­gia sug­gests, Varma said, and now read­ers can com­pare. Specialists write on­line for them­selves, and read­ers who spot a paper’s er­rors in their own field stop trust­ing the rest.
The state, mean­while, wields a stick and a car­rot: raids on owners’ other busi­nesses, sacked ed­i­tors, po­lice vis­its, and gov­ern­ment ad­ver­tis­ing that can be with­drawn. {113-C13}

And at­ten­tion has frag­mented, with al­go­rithms feed­ing each reader more of what they clicked. “Two young peo­ple meet­ing each other is also in a sense two al­go­rithms meet­ing each other,” Varma said. {113-C18}
## No easy an­swers

Varma had promised Shah some hope in the last chap­ter. There was lit­tle. Solo cre­ators on Substack and YouTube now do some of the sense-making, he said, but he could not say who would cover the mu­nic­i­pal­ity and the fly­over.

Shah’s an­swer was firms with busi­ness mod­els. The con­vinc­ing suc­cesses so far, he said, are old media that re­made them­selves: the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and The Economist.

He also re­layed a hope­ful the­ory from his friend Suyash Rai. Radio was a weapon for Hitler and Mussolini be­fore so­ci­eties ab­sorbed it, and today al­most no­body takes WhatsApp for­wards se­ri­ously.
“The peo­ple are not in­def­i­nitely stupid,” Shah said. “The peo­ple are stupid for some time.”

second.label: The page-view era
second.head: A lakh beats a crore
second.deck: At Yahoo India, a Bollywood party photographer outdrew award-winning long-form reporting

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the party photographer who outdrew Originals

body: Around 2009 or 2010, Prem Panicker ran ed­i­to­rial at Yahoo India, where Amit Varma free­lanced for him. The India team was set a tar­get of 500 mil­lion page views a month. {113-S03}
Panicker’s Originals sec­tion pro­duced deeply re­searched long-form re­port­ing on a bud­get of more than a crore a year. Many pieces won awards, and each drew 40,000 or 50,000 page views. {#forty}

Then there was OMG, fed by one Bombay pho­tog­ra­pher paid a lakh a month to shoot Bollywood par­ties. It drew 450 to 500 mil­lion page views on its own. The higher-ups told Panicker his re­turn on in­vest­ment did not com­pare, and Originals was shut down.

quote.text: With that kind of in­vest­ment we are get­ting these kind of page views. Your ROI doesn’t com­pare.

third.head: Show us the paper

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the New Yorker’s fact-checkers

body: When Siddhartha Mukherjee, au­thor of *The Emperor of All Maladies*, wrote in the New Yorker about India’s ex­cess Covid deaths, he in­ter­viewed Ajay Shah over video. Shah had one of the first pa­pers on the sub­ject. {113-S08}

The magazine’s check­ers con­firmed every sen­tence at­trib­uted to him. That was not enough. “Show us the paper. Show us that you have backup for the claims that you made,” Shah re­called them say­ing.

All that for one para­graph of a 20,000-word story. Quality, T.N. Ninan once told Shah, needs enough man-hours at a high enough price per hour. Only Bennett Coleman could af­ford it, and it would not.
So India is stuck, Shah ar­gued: chron­i­cally under-resourced jour­nal­ism pro­duces low qual­ity, and the in­dus­try then con­cludes no­body will pay. {113-C10}

p2.title: Where it went wrong
p2.deck: Amit Varma’s diagnosis, crisis by crisis, with Ajay Shah adding evidence, objections and a little hope

quote.text: A good news­pa­per should be a fil­ter to the truth.

box.title: The voices behind the episode
box.text: To pre­pare, Amit Varma spoke again to three for­mer guests of *The Seen and the Unseen*: Prem Panicker, found­ing man­ag­ing ed­i­tor of Rediff and “a leg­end”, and the younger jour­nal­ists Shephali Bhatt and Samarth Bansal. Credit them for any­thing good, he said. {#three}

sections.label: Crisis One
sections.head: The match you already saw
sections.caption: information that is no longer scarce
body: Journalism is older than the news­pa­per, Amit Varma ar­gued. Town criers and the poets who car­ried oral his­to­ries met three needs: to know what was hap­pen­ing, to pre­serve it and to de­bate it.

Over time it added truth-seeking, sense-making and, in the 20th cen­tury, a watch­dog role. Thucydides, Varma noted, is often called the first jour­nal­ist for how rig­or­ously he checked his sources.
But its found­ing rea­son was scarcity. “Today in­for­ma­tion is abun­dant. There is prac­ti­cally too much in­for­ma­tion. It is no longer a scarce re­source,” he said. {113-C01}
## Ball by ball
Varma had seen this in minia­ture as a cricket writer in the early 2000s. Readers had al­ready watched the match on tele­vi­sion, so the ball-by-ball ac­count had be­come a com­mod­ity. {113-S02}
British pa­pers led the change. Cricket writ­ers had to bring per­spec­tive and colour in­stead, and the writ­ing grew richer.

Today sense-makers are ev­ery­where, Varma said, and many are spe­cial­ists who do the job bet­ter than gen­er­al­ist jour­nal­ists. People swip­ing on Instagram are not at fault; their needs are being met else­where.

Ajay Shah pushed back. Information may be plen­ti­ful, he said, but truth is not: cor­po­ra­tions, gov­ern­ments and po­lit­i­cal par­ties or­gan­ise them­selves to lie, and tribal non­sense such as anti-vax sen­ti­ment spreads.

~ Varma agreed that a good news­pa­per should fil­ter its way to the truth. But his own most trusted fil­ters are in­di­vid­u­als: news­let­ters on Substack, the blog Marginal Revolution, peo­ple he fol­lows on Twitter.

quote.text: A good news­pa­per should be a fil­ter to the truth.

sections.label: Crisis Two
sections.head: Dharma versus the payroll
sections.caption: the editor who would comfort the comforted
body: Every pro­fes­sion has a kind of dharma, Amit Varma said, using the word loosely. Journalism’s higher pur­poses took shape only in the 20th cen­tury: seek­ing truth, speak­ing truth to power, af­flict­ing the com­fort­able and com­fort­ing the af­flicted.
Yet the ed­i­tor of a major Indian news­pa­per told one of the jour­nal­ists Varma spoke to that the job was to com­fort the com­forted. “And he meant it se­ri­ously,” Varma said. {113-S04}

Varma called the state­ment ra­tio­nal. A news­pa­per is a busi­ness, with share­hold­ers and em­ploy­ees to an­swer to. An in­di­vid­ual can put pur­pose be­fore profit; a firm has fidu­ciary du­ties.
## A cost cen­tre

Shephali Bhatt told him that her first news­room, in her early twen­ties, treated jour­nal­ists as a cost cen­tre. Varma also re­called Vineet Jain telling the New Yorker that his com­pany was in the ad­ver­tis­ing busi­ness, not the news busi­ness. {113-C03}
None of this was an ac­cu­sa­tion, Varma in­sisted. “There are no vil­lains in this story,” he said. {#novillains}
~ Ajay Shah re­mem­bered the older bar­gain. In the com­plex where he grew up, jour­nal­ists were poorly paid and there was lit­tle profit in the trade, “but there was a sense of pur­pose”.

quote.text: Vineet Jain fa­mously said to the New Yorker, we are not in the news busi­ness, we are in the ad­ver­tis­ing busi­ness.

sections.label: Crisis Three
sections.head: Printing page views
sections.caption: page views inflated like a currency
body: In the early 2000s, Amit Varma said, ad­ver­tis­ing was the only way to make money on­line. People ex­pected con­tent to be free, as music had been in the days of Napster, and the unit sold was the page view.
As sites mul­ti­plied, so did page views, and each was worth less. “Now in the same way that in the econ­omy, if you in­crease the money sup­ply, in­fla­tion hap­pens,” he said. {113-C04}

The race to the bot­tom brought click­bait, SEO head­lines and pag­i­na­tion, which split an 800-word piece into four pages. As man­ag­ing ed­i­tor of Cricinfo, Varma re­fused. “It is in fact rude to make the reader click again,” he said. {113-S05}
## Where the money went

From 2010 to 2020, Samarth Bansal told him, out­lets such as Vox, Vice and BuzzFeed were promised traf­fic for orig­i­nal con­tent. The ad­ver­tis­ing went to Facebook, YouTube and Instagram in­stead.
For media, Varma said, ad­ver­tis­ing is dead. Writers can now earn from their au­di­ences di­rectly, through sub­scrip­tions, cour­ses and com­mu­ni­ties. {113-C06}

~ Cost-cutting took the beats first: the mu­nic­i­pal­ity, the RBI, the dusty fly­over. Nobody pays for them, but Bansal sees a civic pur­pose in them. “You are writ­ing this first draft of his­tory, which will often be the only draft of his­tory,” Varma said. {113-C09}

quote.text: I don’t need the Times of India and I don’t need ad­ver­tis­ers. I can go di­rectly to my au­di­ence and mon­e­tise my au­di­ence.

sections.label: Crises Four and Five
sections.head: A mile wide, an inch deep
sections.caption: selection bias and Gell-Mann amnesia
body: The qual­ity of Indian jour­nal­ism was never what nos­tal­gia sug­gests, Amit Varma ar­gued. People re­mem­ber Arun Shourie, Vir Sanghvi’s Sunday and India Today’s copy desk under Dilip Bobb, but those were out­liers, and mem­ory is bi­ased to­wards them. {113-S07}
Before the in­ter­net, read­ers had noth­ing to com­pare with, so low stan­dards bred low ex­pec­ta­tions.

Ajay Shah blamed re­sources. Journalists in India are sin­gu­larly un­der­paid, he said, cit­ing his friend Ashima Sharma, and qual­ity takes costly process. The in­dus­try under-invests, pro­duces low qual­ity, and then con­cludes no­body will pay. {113-C10}
He hopes pa­tient in­vestors will fund five years of qual­ity first. Varma is scep­ti­cal.
## Readers who know bet­ter

Trust fell with qual­ity. Varma de­scribed Gell-Mann am­ne­sia: a reader sees that a story on her own field is rub­bish, then trusts the rest of the paper. “Why do you as­sume they re­ported ev­ery­thing else right?” he asked. {113-C11}
Now spe­cial­ists such as Tyler Cowen on eco­nom­ics and Eric Topol on medicine write di­rectly, and read­ers can see the gap.
~ Varma quoted Prem Panicker’s ver­dict: the Indian media is “a mile wide and an inch deep”. {113-J18}

quote.text: We are under in­vest­ing in qual­ity and that cre­ates a chronic in­abil­ity to mon­e­tise and then we are stuck.

sections.label: Crisis Six
sections.head: Asked to bend, they crawled
sections.caption: the state’s stick and carrot
body: Power here means the state, Amit Varma said. During the Emergency, Ramnath Goenka ran a blank page in the Indian Express, but most of the press ca­pit­u­lated. As L.K. Advani put it, “they were asked to bend, they chose to crawl”. {113-J15}

Owners once used their pa­pers as a hedge against the state. The Singhanias started the Indian Post dur­ing their bat­tle with the Wadias. Today, Varma said, cor­po­rate barons buy media houses to do the gov­ern­ment a favour. “You can’t hedge against the state.” {113-C13}
## Stick and car­rot

The stick is pres­sure on owners’ other busi­nesses: a group that also owns chem­i­cal fac­to­ries can be raided by the ED. The car­rot is ad­ver­tis­ing from gov­ern­ment, PSUs and par­ties, which can be with­drawn at any time.

Ajay Shah added con­fer­ence in­come, which de­pends on min­is­ters turn­ing up, and op-ed space handed to serv­ing of­fi­cials. “Why will I pay a sub­scrip­tion for a news­pa­per?” he asked. “If you’re going to give me Doordarshan.” {113-C14}

~ Some in­cen­tives are writ­ten into rules. Varma re­layed Ashok Malik’s ar­gu­ment that tele­vi­sion news shouts be­cause the gov­ern­ment capped what chan­nels could charge sub­scribers, leav­ing them de­pen­dent on ad­ver­tis­ing. {113-C15}

quote.text: A min­is­ter in a gov­ern­ment has the ed­i­tor of one of the big­gest news­pa­pers in the coun­try sum­mar­ily sacked, and he left the coun­try.

sections.label: The future
sections.head: Firms, not lone rangers
sections.caption: who will cover the municipality beat
body: Ajay Shah had found the episode’s plan bleak and asked for some hope at the end. “I said we’ll do it in the last chap­ter. I lied,” Amit Varma said. {113-J05}
The con­di­tions that cre­ated jour­nal­ism and its val­ues are gone, Varma said. The main­stream is crum­bling ev­ery­where, but noth­ing has taken its place.

Solo cre­ators are fill­ing some gaps. On Substack, he noted, “all your email IDs of your sub­scribers ac­tu­ally be­long to you”. {#substack} Dhruv Rathee and Mohak Mangal do sense-making on YouTube.
## Who cov­ers the mu­nic­i­pal­ity?

His worry is the van­ish­ing beat. A local re­porter who goes in­de­pen­dent must learn video, mar­ket­ing and thumb­nails, and will soon be tempted by clicks. Individual pas­sion, he said, pro­duces only a few out­liers. {113-C19}

Shah’s an­swer was firms: teams with a busi­ness model. The con­vinc­ing suc­cesses so far, he said, are old media re­made for the new age, such as the Financial Times, the Wall Street Journal, the New York Times and The Economist.

~ He also re­layed a hope­ful the­ory from Suyash Rai. Radio was a weapon for Mussolini and Hitler be­fore cul­tures ab­sorbed it, and no­body now takes WhatsApp for­wards se­ri­ously. Algorithms may fol­low, if peo­ple learn scep­ti­cism. {113-C20}

quote.text: But you can’t rely on in­di­vid­ual pas­sion and drive be­cause that is a few out­liers.
If you give the reader con­tent, she will scroll. If you keep her at­ten­tion, if you make her in­ter­est­ing, if you give her qual­ity, she will scroll as much as you want her to scroll.

p3.title: Tales from the newsroom
p3.deck: Four stories from the hosts, and what each says about Indian journalism

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah’s childhood in a journalists’ housing complex
stories.head: Eighty households, one calling
body: From the age of six until he left home at 17, Ajay Shah lived in a hous­ing com­plex where 80 house­holds all worked in the Indian media. {#eighty}

It was be­fore tele­vi­sion, so they were all in print, in­clud­ing Hindi, Marathi and Gujarati pa­pers. Amit Varma would not name the fa­mous en­clave, lest “ad­mir­ing nu­bile young women” land up at Shah’s house. {113-J01}

Shah’s fa­ther worked at the Economic Times, which then had a se­ri­ous re­search de­part­ment, the Economic Times Research Bureau. K.A. Antony, for­merly of the RBI, cre­ated it and brought Shah’s fa­ther in; when Antony died, Shah’s fa­ther be­came its sec­ond head.
Top econ­o­mists edited the paper, among them Hanan Ezekiel, “brother of the much more fa­mous Nissim Ezekiel”. {113-J17}

The Times of India grew up around Shamlal and Girilal Jain, whose dense opin­ion pieces the whole coun­try read. Shah com­pared their in­flu­ence to that of France’s philoso­phers in the 1960s. These, he said, were the peo­ple who shaped the col­lec­tive con­scious­ness.

He was ten when the Emergency came. The Indian Express car­ried empty white space rather than print what the cen­sors wanted. {#blank} Later, a full-page in­ves­ti­ga­tion on the Express’s front page by Arun Shourie, into A.R. Antulay’s trusts, cost the Maharashtra chief min­is­ter his job.

~ Journalists were poorly paid, and there was lit­tle profit in the trade. But it was, Shah said, “fully a noble call­ing”. “It was about being good, valu­able par­tic­i­pants in the emer­gence of a good so­ci­ety.”
stories.why: Journalism as a noble call­ing is not a myth: within liv­ing mem­ory, ed­i­tors shaped how a na­tion thought. Varma added a caveat. Such nos­tal­gia is se­lec­tive, he said, and not ev­ery­thing was rosy then. {#rosy}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on growing up among journalists

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the golden age that wasn’t
stories.head: Two words or three?
body: Growing up in the 1980s and 1990s, Amit Varma thought of jour­nal­ism as the place for peo­ple who could not get into en­gi­neer­ing, medicine or the UPSC. Many old-school jour­nal­ists he later worked with could not write a proper English sen­tence.

At the Chinnaswami Stadium in Bangalore, a noted jour­nal­ist from the Hindu, “very nice guy”, once si­dled up to him dur­ing a cricket match. He asked: “Amit, tell me some­thing, is nev­er­the­less two words or three words?” {113-J03}
Varma ad­mits he was ar­ro­gant with some of them, and re­grets it. The leg­ends were real: Arun Shourie, Vir Sanghvi at Sunday, India Today’s copy desk under Dilip Bobb. {113-S07}
~ But be­fore the in­ter­net, read­ers had no New Yorker or Economist to com­pare with. Low stan­dards fed low ex­pec­ta­tions, which fed lower stan­dards.

quote.text: But these are out­liers. This is a se­lec­tion bias play­ing out in our mem­ory. We re­mem­ber the good names.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on the question in the press box

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on what happens when the powerful are annoyed
stories.head: A knock for every byline
body: Amit Varma gave two ex­am­ples of the state’s stick, both from the HT group. When Mint launched, its ed­i­tor Raju Narisetti wrote some­thing that an­gered P. Chidambaram, who had him sacked. Narisetti left the coun­try. {113-S11}
Years later, under the BJP, Bobby Ghosh ran a tracker of hate crimes at the Hindustan Times. Arun Jaitley al­legedly dis­liked it, and Ghosh was sacked too.

Then Shephali Bhatt told Varma about a Financial Times exposé of a lead­ing busi­ness fam­ily. Within a day, po­lice vis­ited every Indian name on the by­line. The for­eign lead cor­re­spon­dent went back to her pre­vi­ous post­ing.
~ And a friend’s in­ves­tiga­tive story, which ev­ery­one called ex­plo­sive, was spiked at the last minute. “But that is the very rea­son it was sort of spiked,” Varma said. {113-J04}
stories.why: The state’s stick is real, used by both par­ties, and works mostly through quiet pres­sure. It ex­plains, Varma said, why small in­de­pen­dent out­lets with noth­ing to lose are often the ones show­ing a spine. {113-J16}
stories.postscript: Varma was un­sure whether “if you ain’t got noth­ing, you got noth­ing to lose” came from Dylan, Joan Baez or Kris Kristofferson.

pic.caption: Amit Varma on sacked editors and police at the door

stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s experiment with the algorithm
stories.head: Separate feeds, separate worlds
body: Amit Varma wanted to see what the kooky right-wing ecosys­tem on YouTube looked like. So he opened an incog­nito win­dow and logged in with an­other Gmail ac­count. {113-S14}
He now has two YouTube feeds. “There has never been a com­mon thing that has come up,” he said. They are dif­fer­ent worlds.

That is his worry about al­go­rithms, which feed you more of what­ever you click. A 15-year-old boy who clicks on one misog­y­nis­tic, rab­ble-rousing piece can end up in a bub­ble of such con­tent, and take it for re­al­ity. {113-C18}

~ When Varma wrote against de­mon­eti­sa­tion in the Times of India, some­one else wrote a col­umn for it, “which is as it should be”. In sep­a­rate feeds, each side will think the other evil, and from in­side its own world, that is rea­son­able.

quote.text: your knowl­edge of the world nar­rows down to one tiny sliver, and even that may not be true.

stories.postscript: Ajay Shah’s an­ti­dote is three printed news­pa­pers each morn­ing, read with cof­fee “like a civilised per­son”.

quiz.a: OMG, a sec­tion of Bollywood party pho­to­graphs from one Bombay pho­tog­ra­pher.

quiz.q: Why did Amit Varma refuse to split articles across several pages at Cricinfo?
quiz.a: Readers scroll for qual­ity con­tent; mak­ing them click again is, he said, rude.

quiz.q: What is Gell-Mann amnesia, the effect Amit Varma described in the trust chapter?
quiz.a: Spotting er­rors on your own sub­ject, then trust­ing the rest of the paper any­way.

quiz.q: Which Indian media company did Ajay Shah call the cleanest test of the clickbait model?
quiz.a: Bennett Coleman: it had the scale, went all in, and its profit de­clined.

quiz.q: Which album did Ajay Shah recommend, and what book inspired it, by his account?
quiz.a: Roger Waters’s *Amused to Death*, writ­ten after Waters read Neil Postman’s book.

glossary.def: A blast: what ev­ery­one called the friend’s spiked in­ves­ti­ga­tion.
Trusting a paper after see­ing it botch your own field.
To state the op­pos­ing view as well as its holder would.
Splitting one ar­ti­cle across pages to mul­ti­ply page views.
Reporting with ac­cess granted, and coloured, by the state.
Tracing ex­actly which click led to which sale.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 113. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Murray Gell-Mann (World Economic Forum, CC BY-SA 2.0); Walter Lippmann (Pirie MacDonald, public domain); Marshall McLuhan (Josephine Smith, public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: Public Opinion
shelf.creator: Walter Lippmann
shelf.why: Lippmann’s cen­tury-old mas­ter­piece on how the media shapes what we be­lieve and what to watch out for, which no tech­no­log­i­cal change has made ob­so­lete; Amit says ev­ery­one should read it.

shelf.title: Understanding Media
shelf.creator: Marshall McLuhan
shelf.why: Amit calls it ab­so­lutely worth read­ing for any­one think­ing about how media shapes us.

shelf.title: Amusing Ourselves to Death
shelf.creator: Neil Postman
shelf.why: It com­pletes his read­ing list on the media, which fits an episode about sen­sa­tion­al­ism, frag­mented at­ten­tion and media as en­ter­tain­ment.

shelf.title: Amused to Death
shelf.creator: Roger Waters
shelf.why: Ajay says Roger Waters read Neil Postman’s book and then wrote the album, so it is a mu­si­cal com­pan­ion to Postman’s ar­gu­ment.

shelf.title: The age of the partial outsider
shelf.creator: Janan Ganesh
shelf.why: It names a use­ful stance: being close enough to a field to have in­flu­ence but out­side enough not to be bound by its con­ven­tions.

shelf.title: The State of the Media (Episode 46 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Prem Panicker)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit says Prem’s episodes with him are re­ally good.

shelf.title: The Prem Panicker Files (Episode 217 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: More of Prem’s first-hand ex­pe­ri­ence of how Indian media changed, from the man Amit calls a leg­end.

shelf.title: Shephali Bhatt Is Searching for the Incredible (Episode 391 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Journalist Shephali Bhatt on find­ing her sense of pur­pose through in­di­vid­u­als in news­rooms that treated jour­nal­ists as a cost cen­tre, which Amit finds very mov­ing.

shelf.title: The Reflections of Samarth Bansal (Episode 299 of The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Samarth is the source of the ideas of ‘civic purpose’, ‘in­vis­i­ble quitting’, and India’s ‘shal­low ecosystem’ of media ex­per­i­ments.

shelf.title: Citizens Jain
shelf.creator: Ken Auletta
shelf.why: It is the source of the line that cap­tures how a big media com­pany de­fines its own pur­pose.

shelf.title: An Adman Reflects on Society & the Self (Episode 199 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ambi Paramaeswaran)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Here ad­ver­tis­ing leg­end Ambi Paramaeswaran said that far more than half of ad spend is wasted and that on­line ad­ver­tis­ing is a scan­dal.

shelf.title: How to Think About Cricket (and Life) (Episode 19)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit’s con­trar­ian ideas on cricket strat­egy and tac­tics, first de­vel­oped in 2008 and still not well un­der­stood, which he says hold truly novel in­sights.

shelf.title: Why Does the Pandemic Seem to Be Hitting Some Countries Harder Than Others?
shelf.creator: Siddhartha Mukherjee
shelf.why: It led to Ajay’s first-hand ex­pe­ri­ence of the New Yorker’s fact-checking, his main ex­am­ple of what real ed­i­to­rial process in­volves.

shelf.title: Gell-Mann Amnesia
shelf.creator: Michael Crichton
shelf.why: Crichton’s ex­pla­na­tion of Gell-Mann Amnesia: we catch the media get­ting our own field wrong, then trust it on ev­ery­thing else.

shelf.title: The WSJ story on Trump
shelf.creator: The Wall Street Journal
shelf.why: Ajay uses it as an ex­am­ple of jour­nal­ism you can trust: a paper wouldn’t take on some­one fa­mous for suing with­out doing the hard work.

shelf.title: Television Price Controls (Episode 27 of The Seen and the Unseen, with Ashok Malik)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Ashok Malik ex­plains why Indian TV news is so bad: gov­ern­ment price caps on sub­scrip­tions forced chan­nels to de­pend on ad­ver­tis­ing and race to the bot­tom.

shelf.title: The World in 2050 (Episode 106)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: A play­ful but se­ri­ous at­tempt to imag­ine the world 25 years out, from swarms of cheap drones in war to how re­la­tion­ships might be or­gan­ised once love, sex, com­pan­ion­ship and par­ent­ing come apart.

shelf.title: Persuasion
shelf.creator: Yascha Mounk
shelf.why: It shows in­de­pen­dent cre­ators build­ing se­ri­ous pub­li­ca­tions out­side main­stream media.

shelf.title: The Free Press
shelf.creator: Bari Weiss
shelf.why: Bari Weiss’s pub­li­ca­tion, ev­i­dence that one per­son start­ing a news­let­ter can build a very large busi­ness on plat­forms where cre­ators own their au­di­ence, with­out a mass-media gate­keeper.

shelf.title: Dhruv Rathee’s YouTube channel
shelf.creator: Dhruv Rathee
shelf.why: Amit sets aside the ques­tion of qual­ity, but says his num­bers show huge de­mand for the fil­ter­ing and sense-making that main­stream media should be pro­vid­ing.

shelf.title: Mohak Mangal’s YouTube channel
shelf.creator: Mohak Mangal
shelf.why: Amit says he works hard and does a pretty good job of the sense-making func­tion.

shelf.title: Marginal Revolution
shelf.creator: Tyler Cowen and Alex Tabarrok
shelf.why: The blog Amit thinks has been the best in the world for 15 years: two econ­o­mists think­ing aloud in clear prose every day, a model for aca­demics and bet­ter sense-making than a newspaper’s eco­nom­ics pages.

shelf.title: Eric Topol’s writing on medicine
shelf.creator: Eric Topol
shelf.why: To un­der­stand cut­ting-edge medicine, Amit would read Topol on Twitter, in his ar­ti­cles or in his books rather than the Times of India.

shelf.title: The Art of Clear Writing
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s writ­ing course, which treats clear writ­ing as a test of clear think­ing.

shelf.title: Life Lessons
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Amit and Ajay’s course on what they wish they had been taught at twenty: learn­ing how to learn, frame­works for think­ing, writ­ing, prob­a­bilis­tic in­tu­ition, eco­nom­ics, the his­tory of thought, per­sonal fi­nance (Ajay’s mod­ule is ‘legendary’) and health.

laughs.text: Amit re­fuses to name the fa­mous journalists’ hous­ing en­clave where Ajay grew up: ‘We won’t take the name be­cause we don’t want ad­mir­ing nu­bile young women to land up at your house if we ac­ci­den­tally give the ad­dress away.’

When Amit de­scribed him­self as a per­pet­ual out­sider, Ajay called him ‘The mighty pod­caster who will not join any club that will have him.’ Amit replied: ‘I’m re­ally glad, re­ally glad for once that you quoted the right Marx. This of course is Groucho Marx, right? So well done.’

Amit’s grow­ing-up view of jour­nal­ism: it was where society’s re­jects went, the peo­ple who couldn’t get into en­gi­neer­ing, medicine or the UPSC. One noted Hindu jour­nal­ist si­dled up to him in the Chinnaswami press box and asked, ‘Amit, tell me some­thing, is nev­er­the­less two words or three words?’
After Ajay called the episode plan bleak and asked for some­thing hope­ful, Amit says: ‘I said we’ll do it in the last chap­ter. I lied.’

Amit on phones: ‘I’m not say­ing ev­ery­thing we do on our phones is wrong. It’s only about 99.8% is wrong.’ He then goes off on a ‘like and subscribe’ tan­gent (‘Ajay looks at the num­bers. So let’s see if my say­ing this moves the nee­dle... If it does, we’ll say it in every episode. No, we won’t’), loses his thread, and ad­mits: ‘My at­ten­tion went to hell. See what just hap­pened, these are bad habits.’
Amit in­ter­rupts Ajay’s vi­sion of media firms full of spe­cial­ists: ‘I just want to in­ter­rupt and say no one knows how to make thumb­nails. Everybody’s wing­ing it.’
Asked how The Seen and the Unseen is doing after going fort­nightly, Amit says he hasn’t checked the num­bers in a year and a half: ‘I do the work I do. I’m not a cir­cus mon­key.’

When Ajay rec­om­mends Roger Waters’ Amused to Death, Amit says he’s ‘just pig­gy­back­ing on words.’ Ajay ex­plains that Waters read the Postman book be­fore writ­ing it. Asked if he made that up, he says: ‘No no se­ri­ously I’m not just an LLM.’
Thucydides, the an­cient his­to­rian Amit says is often called the first jour­nal­ist be­cause of how rig­or­ously he ver­i­fied his sources.

John Wanamaker’s line that half the money spent on ad­ver­tis­ing is wasted and no­body knows which half. Ambi Paramaeswaran told Amit it’s much more than half, and that what ad­ver­tis­ers do on­line is a scan­dal that sim­ply isn’t work­ing.
L.K. Advani on the press dur­ing the Emergency: ‘they were asked to bend, they chose to crawl’, set against Ramnath Goenka’s blank page in the Indian Express.

‘If you ain’t got noth­ing, you got noth­ing to lose’, quoted by Amit, who wasn’t sure whether it came from Dylan, Joan Baez or Kris Kristofferson, to ex­plain why small in­de­pen­dent out­lets are the ones show­ing a spine.

Hanan Ezekiel, ‘brother of the much more fa­mous Nissim Ezekiel, but re­ally one of the best econ­o­mists of India’, once edited the Economic Times. Ajay com­pares that era’s ed­i­tors to France’s 1960s philoso­phers.
Prem Panicker’s ver­dict, quoted by Amit: the Indian media is ‘a mile wide and an inch deep’.
The clas­sic jour­nal­is­tic motto ‘af­flict the com­fort­able, com­fort the afflicted’, and jour­nal­ism as ‘the first draft of history’, which Amit ex­tends to ‘often the only draft of history’.
